name: Joachim Sauer
milestone_by_age_26: Earned doctorate in chemistry in 1974 at age 25, but no material, independently notable milestone by 26; major scientific recognition (Liebig Medal 2010, Schrödinger Medal 2019, Royal Society membership 2018) came decades later.

name: Jairzinho
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 1970 FIFA World Cup with Brazil at age 25, scoring in every game of the tournament—a feat only one other player had achieved in World Cup history.
early_history_summary: Jairzinho joined Botafogo's youth academy at age 13 in 1958 and made his professional debut at 15 in 1960. He established himself as a Botafogo regular by 1965 at age 21, eventually replacing Garrincha on the right wing for both club and country, and won the 1968 Brazilian double with Botafogo before his historic 1970 World Cup performance.
family_context_summary: Jairzinho's family left Duque de Caxias for Rio de Janeiro in the late 1950s; he lived on Rua General Severiano near Botafogo's stadium. No specific family financial or professional background is documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Botafogo youth academy, Rio de Janeiro football ecosystem, Garrincha succession, Brazilian national team
evidence_summary: Jairzinho grew up near Botafogo's stadium in Rio de Janeiro and entered the club's youth system at 13, making his professional debut at 15. He was immersed in one of the world's most competitive football ecosystems, training alongside Brazilian stars like Garrincha, Gérson, and Mario Zagallo at Botafogo. His exceptional physical talent—pace, power, and finishing—was evident from his teenage years, and by 25 he had become a World Cup champion scoring in every match. No family financial or domain advantage is documented in reviewed sources.

name: Paolo Maldini
milestone_by_age_26: Made his Serie A debut for AC Milan on 20 January 1985 at age 16, became a starting eleven member at 17, and by 26 had won multiple Serie A titles, two European Cups, and been named best under-23 player in European competitions.
early_history_summary: Maldini joined AC Milan's youth academy at age 10 in 1978 and made his Serie A debut at 16 under manager Nils Liedholm. He was immediately integrated into the starting lineup at 17, inheriting the number 3 shirt previously worn by his father Cesare, and by his early 20s was a cornerstone of one of football's greatest defensive units alongside Franco Baresi and Alessandro Costacurta.
family_context_summary: Maldini is the son of Cesare Maldini, AC Milan legend who captained the club to its first European Cup in 1963 and later managed the Italian national team. The family was comfortably middle class, immersed in professional football from Paolo's birth.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Cesare Maldini was a legendary AC Milan captain and Italian international who won four Serie A titles and the European Cup. Paolo inherited his father's number 3 shirt at Milan, creating a direct family-domain pipeline into elite football.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Cesare Maldini son, AC Milan youth academy, number 3 shirt inheritance, Baresi defensive partnership, Serie A ecosystem
evidence_summary: Paolo Maldini was born into one of football's most storied family legacies: his father Cesare captained AC Milan to its first European Cup and later managed Italy. Paolo joined Milan's youth academy at 10, made his Serie A debut at 16, and inherited his father's number 3 shirt at 17. He was embedded in the world's strongest defensive unit alongside Franco Baresi and Alessandro Costacurta, and grew up in Milan at the height of Serie A's global prominence. The family-domain advantage was exceptionally direct—same club, same position, same shirt number.

name: Brian Josephson
milestone_by_age_26: Discovered the Josephson effect in 1962 at age 22 as a PhD student at Cambridge, predicting that a supercurrent could tunnel through a thin barrier—a discovery that won him the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physics.
early_history_summary: Josephson attended Cardiff High School where a physics master introduced him to theoretical physics. He went to Cambridge at 17, published influential papers as an undergraduate including one on the Mössbauer effect, and as a PhD student under Brian Pippard in 1962 discovered the Josephson effect, which was experimentally confirmed at Bell Labs in 1963.
family_context_summary: Josephson was born to Jewish parents Abraham Josephson and Mimi Weisbard in Cardiff, Wales. No specific family financial or professional background is documented in reviewed sources beyond this.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Cambridge Cavendish Laboratory, Trinity College, Brian Pippard supervision, Philip Anderson mentorship, quantum physics frontier
evidence_summary: Josephson was recognized as a brilliant student from his school days in Cardiff, where a physics master introduced him to theoretical physics. At Cambridge, he was embedded in the world's leading condensed matter physics environment—the Cavendish Laboratory under Brian Pippard, with future Nobel laureate Philip Anderson as a visiting professor. His exceptional cognitive ability was noted by examiners and colleagues alike. As a 22-year-old PhD student, he predicted the Josephson effect, which was experimentally confirmed within months and eventually earned him the Nobel Prize. No family financial or domain advantage is documented.

name: Joop Zoetemelk
milestone_by_age_26: Won a gold medal in the 100km team time trial at the 1968 Summer Olympics in Mexico City at age 22, and won the 1969 Tour de l'Avenir before turning professional in 1970.
early_history_summary: Zoetemelk started as a speed skater and regional champion before turning to cycling in 1964 at age 18. He joined the Swift club in Leiden, quickly won youth races, and excelled in multi-day races, winning the Tour of Yugoslavia, Circuit des Mines, and stages at the Tour of Austria before his Olympic gold and Tour de l'Avenir victories.
family_context_summary: Zoetemelk was the son of Maria and Gerard Zoetemelk and was raised in Rijpwetering, Netherlands. He started his working life as a carpenter before pursuing cycling. No specific family financial or domain background is documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Dutch cycling culture, Swift club Leiden, Olympic team, speed skating background
evidence_summary: Zoetemelk came from a working-class background in the Netherlands, starting as a carpenter before turning to cycling at 18. He benefited from the Netherlands' strong cycling culture and the national team program, but no family financial or domain advantages are documented. His speed skating background provided transferable physical conditioning. He won Olympic gold in the team time trial at 22, benefiting from strong teammates, and went on to a dominant professional career including a Tour de France victory in 1980.

name: Plácido Domingo
milestone_by_age_26: Made his first leading operatic role as Alfredo in La traviata in Monterrey in 1961 at age 20, sang 280 performances of 12 roles with the Israel National Opera by 1965, and created the title role in the US premiere of Ginastera's Don Rodrigo at New York City Opera in 1966 to critical acclaim.
early_history_summary: Domingo was born to zarzuela singer parents who moved to Mexico when he was 8 and started their own zarzuela company. He studied piano and voice at the National Conservatory of Music in Mexico City from age 14, made his professional debut at 16 accompanying his mother on piano, and his operatic debut at 18 at the Palacio de Bellas Artes before launching an international career.
family_context_summary: Domingo was born to Pepita Embil and Plácido Domingo Ferrer, both professional zarzuela singers who started their own zarzuela company in Mexico after a successful Latin American tour. The family was immersed in musical theater from his birth, and his parents recruited him and his sister for children's roles in their productions.
parent_family_domain_summary: Both parents were professional zarzuela performers: his father was a violinist and baritone, his mother a singer. They created a family zarzuela company in Mexico, providing Domingo with direct immersion in performance, repertoire, and the music profession from early childhood.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Zarzuela singer parents, family company, National Conservatory of Music, Palacio de Bellas Artes, Israel National Opera, 280 performances
evidence_summary: Domingo was born into a family of professional zarzuela performers who relocated to Mexico to start their own company, giving him direct immersion in musical performance from early childhood. He entered the National Conservatory of Music at 14, made his professional debut at 16, and by 20 was singing leading operatic roles. His parents' company provided a platform for early performing experience, and his training at the conservatory under Carlo Morelli gave him formal vocal technique. By 25, he had accumulated 280 performances across 12 roles at the Israel National Opera, an extraordinary volume of early reps that established him as a major talent.

name: Grigori Perelman
milestone_by_age_26: Won a gold medal with a perfect score at the 1982 International Mathematical Olympiad at age 16, earned his PhD in 1990 at 24, and won the Young Mathematician Prize of the Saint Petersburg Mathematical Society in 1991 at age 25 for his work on Alexandrov spaces.
early_history_summary: Perelman's mathematical talent was apparent by age 10, when his mother enrolled him in Sergei Rukshin's after-school mathematics program. He attended Leningrad Secondary School 239, a specialized math and physics school, won a perfect-score gold medal at the 1982 IMO at 16, and continued at Leningrad State University before completing his PhD in 1990 under Aleksandr Aleksandrov and Yuri Burago.
family_context_summary: Perelman was born to Jewish parents in Leningrad. His mother Lyubov gave up graduate work in mathematics to raise him, creating a mathematically oriented household. His father Yakov later moved to Israel. The family's Jewish identity in the Soviet Union may have created institutional friction.
parent_family_domain_summary: His mother Lyubov was a mathematician who sacrificed her own graduate studies to raise him, providing early mathematical exposure. His father Yakov's profession is not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Rukshin math program, School 239, Leningrad mathematical school, mother mathematician, IMO gold perfect score, Burago and Aleksandrov advisors
evidence_summary: Perelman's mathematical talent was identified at age 10 by his mother, herself a mathematician who had abandoned graduate study, who enrolled him in Sergei Rukshin's intensive after-school mathematics program. He attended Leningrad's specialized School 239 and won a perfect-score gold medal at the 1982 IMO at 16. He was then embedded in the Leningrad mathematical tradition under Aleksandr Aleksandrov and Yuri Burago, with Mikhail Gromov as a key recommender. His mother's mathematical background provided early domain exposure, though no financial advantage is documented. Being Jewish in the Soviet Union may have created institutional friction that sharpened his focus.

name: Richard Dawkins
milestone_by_age_26: Completed DPhil at Oxford by 1966 at age 25 and began as assistant professor at UC Berkeley in 1967, but these are standard academic career steps; his influential work 'The Selfish Gene' was published in 1976 at age 35.

name: Michel Mayor
milestone_by_age_26: Completed MS in Physics from University of Lausanne in 1966 at age 24; no material, independently notable milestone by 26. His Nobel Prize-winning discovery of 51 Pegasi b, the first exoplanet orbiting a sun-like star, came in 1995 at age 53.

name: Anna Wintour
milestone_by_age_26: Worked as an editorial assistant at Harper's & Queen from 1970 and became a junior fashion editor at Harper's Bazaar in New York in 1975 at age 26, but these are early-career positions; her transformative role as editor-in-chief of Vogue came in 1988 at age 39.

name: Shing-Tung Yau
milestone_by_age_26: Completed his PhD in mathematics at UC Berkeley in 1971 at age 22 under Shiing-Shen Chern with a generalization of Preissman's theorem, became assistant professor at Stony Brook at 23, and associate professor at Stanford at 25.
early_history_summary: Yau was born in China and moved to Hong Kong as an infant, where his family faced financial hardship and his father died when he was 13. He studied mathematics at the Chinese University of Hong Kong from 1966 to 1969, left before graduating due to exceptional ability, and entered the PhD program at UC Berkeley in 1969, completing his doctorate in just two years under Shiing-Shen Chern.
family_context_summary: Yau was born to Han Chinese Hakka parents in Shantou, China. His father Chen Ying Chiu was a Kuomintang scholar of philosophy, history, literature, and economics. The family moved to Hong Kong when Yau was an infant, losing all their possessions. His father and second-oldest sister died when he was 13, creating severe financial hardship. He was the fifth of eight children.
parent_family_domain_summary: His father was a scholar of philosophy, history, literature, and economics whose books Yau began reading after his father's death. While not a mathematician, the scholarly household environment provided intellectual stimulation. The family's financial collapse after moving to Hong Kong meant no material advantage.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Shiing-Shen Chern advisor, UC Berkeley, Stephen Salaff recommendation, IBM Fellowship, IAS Princeton, father scholar, financial hardship, stateless
evidence_summary: Yau's family lost all possessions fleeing to Hong Kong, and his father died when he was 13, creating severe financial hardship. Despite this, his father's scholarly background gave him intellectual exposure, and a lecturer at the Chinese University of Hong Kong named Stephen Salaff recognized his exceptional mathematical potential and helped him gain admission to Berkeley with an IBM Fellowship. Under Shiing-Shen Chern, one of the world's leading geometers, Yau completed his PhD in two years at age 22. He then moved through IAS Princeton, Stony Brook, and Stanford in rapid succession. The combination of exceptional ability, elite mentorship, and adversity-driven focus propelled him to a Fields Medal by age 33.

name: Carlos Monzón
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Argentine middleweight championship in 1966 at age 24 and the South American middleweight championship in 1967 at age 25, establishing himself as a rising international contender before winning the undisputed world middleweight title in 1970.
early_history_summary: Monzón was born into extreme poverty in San Javier, Argentina, with 12 siblings, and quit school in the third grade to work as a shoeshine, paperboy, and milkman. He supplemented his income with street fights before entering amateur boxing, compiling a 73-6-8 record, and turned professional in 1963 at age 20 under the mentorship of trainer Amilcar Brusa.
family_context_summary: Monzón was born to Roque Monzón and Amalia Ledesma, of Mocoví indigenous descent, and was raised in poverty with twelve siblings in a poor neighborhood of Santa Fe. The family was so poor that Monzón could not afford boxing boots early in his career and he and his wife could not afford a marriage license.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. No family connection to boxing or professional sports is recorded.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Extreme poverty, Mocoví descent, street fighting, Amilcar Brusa mentorship, Argentine boxing tradition, self-made
evidence_summary: Monzón grew up in extreme poverty in provincial Argentina, of Mocoví indigenous descent, with twelve siblings. He quit school in third grade to work menial jobs and earned extra money through street fights before finding amateur boxing. His trainer Amilcar Brusa, an ex-wrestler, provided sustained mentorship that channeled his natural fighting ability into boxing technique. The adversity of his upbringing—poverty, lack of education, street violence—created the urgency and physical toughness that propelled him to Argentine and South American middleweight titles by 25. No family financial or domain advantages are documented; his path was entirely self-created through physical talent and constraint-driven determination.
